lesson.title: Whose Priority Is It Anyway: Net Neutrality and the Politics of QoS
lesson.summary: Net neutrality is the policy principle that internet providers should treat all traffic passing through their networks equally, which puts it in direct tension with the very QoS mechanisms this unit has been building toward.
lesson.body:
Every mechanism covered so far in this unit, traffic shaping, token bucket and leaky bucket, fair queuing, scheduling disciplines, admission control, DiffServ, and IntServ, exists to answer one purely technical question: given limited link capacity, which packets go first? Net neutrality asks a related but genuinely different question about those same tools: who gets to decide the answer, and on what basis are they allowed to decide it?

The principle itself holds that an internet service provider carrying traffic to and from its subscribers should not block, throttle, or grant paid prioritization to specific applications, content, or sources. Concretely, this means an ISP should not slow down a competing video-streaming service while exempting its own service from the same data caps, and should not charge a content provider extra money to have that provider's packets scheduled ahead of everyone else's packets on the very same shared link.

The tension with everything covered earlier in this unit can be stated precisely. DiffServ's Expedited Forwarding marking, a strict priority scheduling discipline, and an admission control check are all technically indistinguishable whether they are used to give a latency-sensitive voice or video call the treatment it legitimately needs, or used instead to give one company's traffic a paid advantage over a competitor's traffic for purely commercial reasons unrelated to congestion. The exact same Per Hop Behavior that keeps a video call sounding clear can, applied selectively for the wrong reason, become the actual mechanism of anticompetitive discrimination. QoS, in other words, is a neutral toolbox. Net neutrality is a policy question about who is allowed to use that toolbox, and why.

A little regulatory grounding, stated carefully rather than exhaustively: in the United States, the FCC adopted open internet rules in 2015 that reclassified broadband under stronger regulatory authority, and then largely repealed those rules in an order that took effect in 2018, so the legal status of net neutrality in the US has shifted as administrations changed. Other jurisdictions, including the European Union, have adopted their own open internet regulations along similar lines. What stays constant underneath any of that regulatory back and forth is the technical reality: a real network occasionally needs to prioritize congestion-sensitive traffic, like a live voice call competing against a large background download, and that operational need does not disappear just because net neutrality rules are in effect. Most net neutrality frameworks explicitly carve out an allowance for what they call reasonable network management, using mechanisms exactly like the scheduling disciplines and DiffServ classes covered earlier in this unit. What such frameworks aim to prohibit is not congestion management itself, but prioritization sold to the highest bidder or withheld from a competitor for commercial advantage that has nothing to do with actually managing congestion.
